verdicts.trueWording: of little use to an understanding of the narrative
verdicts.note: Inside a block quote closing '(Wright, Attending Daedalus 139-140)', diss. ch. 1 (~p.7); Wright's own words about Wolfe's multiple allusions being largely external to the text.

verdicts.trueWording: the diction of each text is 'suggestive rather than definitive'
verdicts.note: Aramini, ch. 1, reporting Wright (AD 188) on Wolfe's mistranslations/substitutions as translator; 'each text' = the two texts framed as Wolfe's translations.

verdicts.trueWording: his deliberately mannered and archaic idiom a deterrent
verdicts.note: Block quote from Roberts in diss. ch. 1 (~p.6): 'although some find...'. Source field's book title is loose - the Works Cited names Palgrave History of Science Fiction, 2nd ed. 2016.

verdicts.trueWording: rely too much on over-lengthy and expository dialogue
verdicts.note: Same Roberts block quote, ch. 1; subject is 'his more recent books', matching the claim's 'later books'.

verdicts.trueWording: Usually in a high and archaic register, it would lapse
verdicts.note: Wizard Knight chapter (~p.137), quoting the reviewer the diss. identifies as Professor Stephen Frug of Cornell; the criticism is aimed at Able's voice, called 'profoundly uneven'.

verdicts.trueWording: the mixture of slang into otherwise unbroken pages of high-register speech
verdicts.note: Same Frug block quote, Wizard Knight chapter; that clause ends by calling the mixture frequently awkward in the extreme, covering both dialogue and narration.

verdicts.trueWording: their meaning is not always immediately obvious
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the unqualified 'their meaning is not immediately obvious' - the page says 'not always'
verdicts.note: Aramini's own sentence (~p.36, ch. 1) reads 'Symbols are rigorous and logical in Wolfe's hands, but' then the quoted clause; the rigorous-and-logical limb is fully supported, only the dropped hedge is not.

verdicts.trueWording: he abandons the baroque and long sentences
verdicts.note: Interview answer on how Wolfe's style develops: the transformation is placed 'after the publication of The Book of the New Sun'.

verdicts.trueWording: often strives for a more minimalistic surface text
verdicts.note: Same interview sentence as index 1150, so 'later work' = post-New Sun work.

verdicts.trueWording: The subtext tends to replace the text
verdicts.note: Interview, immediately after Aramini calls the post-Wizard Knight novels hard to get to the bottom of; 'late novels' is that referent.

verdicts.trueWording: something is true about almost every detail which is included
verdicts.note: Interview, in the 'I assume that Wolfe understands the motivations of his characters' sentence, so the working-assumption limb is explicit; ends 'in the text'.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe writes with the precision of an engineer
verdicts.note: Interview answer on how his approach differs from other critics; prefaced 'One of my starting principles was that', i.e. one of several, past tense.

verdicts.trueWording: creates symbols and metaphors to produce concrete plot conclusions
verdicts.note: Interview, closing the list of Wolfe's sophisticated techniques (mise en abyme, embedded tales, allusions).

verdicts.trueWording: I provide a summary with 'mostly' objective details
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that this holds for his entries generally - the page scopes the summary-then-analysis format to the short stories
verdicts.note: Interview: summary, then analysis of deeper or symbolic connections, then allusion sections - but the next sentences say that was the structure for the short stories, while for the longer works he chose a thesis and built the write-up round it.

verdicts.trueWording: Robert Borski takes too many leaps to follow logically
verdicts.note: Interview, same sentence: Andre-Driussi is credited with a good approach that avoids taking major risks, supporting the 'sound' limb.
